podcast.title: Lymphoma Diagnosis (1994)
podcast.body: In 1994, Joey Ramone was diagnosed with lymphoma. This was an "open secret" within his close New York circle, and he managed the disease with treatment and medication for several years. "Sometime in 1994, Joey was diagnosed with lymphoma."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Accidental Hip Fracture (December 30, 2000)
podcast.body: On a cold and icy December 30, 2000, Joey Ramone, compelled by an OCD urge, slipped and fell on the ice while crossing the city, breaking his hip. His bones had been made brittle by his ongoing chemotherapy treatments, exacerbating the injury. "On December 30, 2000, he was overwhelmed with a feeling that he hadn't closed a door on the other side of the city...Joey slipped and fell on the ice...he broke his hip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Cessation of Lymphoma Treatment (December 2000)
podcast.body: The hip surgery required after Joey Ramone's fall necessitated a halt to his lymphoma treatments. This interruption caused the disease to come out of remission, making it untreatable and leading to his eventual death. "This required surgery. And that required he stopped his lymphoma treatments. The disease came out of remission and couldn't be beaten back."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 8: (30-21)

podcast.title: Hip Break Incident (2000)
podcast.body: On December 30, 2000, while walking down a street in New York City, Joey Ramone fell and broke his hip. This severe injury necessitated taking him off his chemotherapy treatment so he could undergo surgery.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Hip Fracture and Cancer Complications (2000-2001)
podcast.body: On December 30th, 2000, while undergoing chemotherapy for lymphoma, Joey slipped on ice outside his building due to his poor vision and broke his hip. This injury necessitated the temporary cessation of his immune-system-weakening cancer drugs for surgery. He was briefly discharged in February 2001 but soon returned to the hospital, never again returning to his apartment. The lymphatic cancer aggressively attacked his immune system, leaving him vulnerable to infection. "On December 30th, 2000, after moving home during some chemotherapy sessions for his lymphoma, he left his building and didn't see the ice on the sidewalk. He slipped, he fell, and he broke his hip. As a result, doctors had to take him off his cancer-fighting drugs, drugs that weakened his immune system so he could undergo surgery for this badly broken hip. He was released for a few days in February, but he was soon back in the hospital. He never went back to his apartment again. The lymphatic cancer then went after Joey's immune system, but he was all but shutting it down and leaving him susceptible to infection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death (April 15, 2001)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone passed away on April 15, 2001, a month before his 50th birthday. His death was caused by lymphoma, which had re-emerged aggressively after he was forced to stop treatments following a hip injury, making him the first original Ramones member to die. "And on April 15, 2001, a month before his 50th birthday, Joey Ramon passed away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death from Lymphoma (2001)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone, considered by some to be perhaps the most influential punk rocker ever, died after a long battle with lymphoma. His illness had been an "open secret" for years, and he had seemed stable until a critical incident in late 2000.

podcast.title: Death on April 15, 2001
podcast.body: Joey Ramone passed away on April 15th, 2001, following complications from lymphatic cancer, which had severely compromised his immune system. "And he died on April 15th, 2001."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Final Decline and Death (2001)
podcast.body: Following a brief release in February 2001, Joey Ramone returned to Presbyterian Hospital in New York. As his hip healed, the cancer aggressively returned, systematically destroying his immune system and leading to severe infection. He never left the hospital again, and his family was called to his room on Sunday, April 15, 2001, where he passed away at 2:40 PM.

podcast.title: Gentle Nature and Untimely Death (2001)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone was described as a tremendously gentle, shy, and sweet individual. He died in April 2001 from complications related to lymphoma, unmarried and without children. "When Joey died in April 2001 of complications from lymphoma, he was unmarried and had no kids."

podcast.title: Admiration for Charles Manson
podcast.body: Joey Ramone expressed admiration for Charles Manson, with his brother quoting him as saying, "He's like Hitler, only cooler." "He was an admirer of Charles Manson. Here's a quote. He's like Hitler, only cooler. This is according to Joey's brother, by the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Astute Stock Market Investor
podcast.body: Financially, Joey Ramone was "probably doing the best" among the Ramones members, making a significant portion of his money through the stock market, in addition to royalties from songs like "I Wanna Be Sedated" and "Blitzkrieg Bop." In his later years, he amassed "quite a fortune" by trading stocks online from his apartment at 115 East 9th Street in Manhattan, watching business channels for entertainment. "But Joey was really making his money in the stock market."

podcast.title: Childhood Violent Incident and Mental Ward Stay
podcast.body: As a child, Joey was described as "out of control." During an altercation with his mother, he held a knife to her throat, an incident that led to him being admitted to a mental ward for a month. "When he was a kid, Joey was really out of control. He once got into a fight with his mom and put a knife to her throat. That landed him in a mental ward for a month."

podcast.title: Comparison to Joe Strummer's Impact
podcast.body: Joe Strummer's influence and significance for a generation were likened to that of Joey Ramone, placing him among the foundational figures of punk rock whose passing marked a generational shift. "To many Joe Strummer was their equivalent of Kurt Cobain, just as Joey Ramon might have been."

podcast.body: Joey Ramone died from lymphoma, which spread throughout his body after he fell and broke his hip, forcing him to discontinue his chemotherapy treatment. "he ended up dying of lymphoma, which overtook his body when he fell and broke his hip, forcing him to stop his chemo."

podcast.title: Doctor's Personality Assessment and Diagnosis
podcast.body: Medical professionals observed Joey as having low self-esteem, perceiving himself as both dangerous and in danger. He approached the unfamiliar with caution and suspicion, often exhibiting poor judgment. They described his self-perception as passive and dependent, with ambivalent sexual identification, which he defended against through distancing behaviors. His view of authority was marked by fear, believing his life to be in danger. His personality structure was deemed consistent with a diagnosis of schizophrenia, paranoid type, accompanied by minimal, likely long-standing, brain damage. "The patient essentially sees himself with low self-esteem as a combination of being both dangerous and in danger, approaching the unfamiliar with considerable caution and suspicion, frequently employing poor judgment in the process. His sense of self is of a passive, dependent person with ambivalent sexual identification, against which he is inclined to defend himself by means of distancing maneuvers to the point of a strangement. His view of authority is markedly fearful, feeling his life to be in danger. The patient's personality structure is consistent with diagnosis of schizophrenia, paranoid type, with minimal brain damage. The latter, probably of long-standing duration."

podcast.title: Earlier Psychotic Break
podcast.body: When he was younger, Joey Ramone experienced a psychotic break that necessitated hospitalization. This personal history of mental health challenges significantly influenced the thematic content of many Ramones songs, which frequently explored concepts related to the brain, psychiatry, shock treatments, and sedation. "When he was younger, he had some kind of psychotic break, which resulted in hospitalization."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Drumming & Influences – Beatles and Keith Moon
podcast.body: Growing up, Jeff Hyman (later Joey Ramone) was a big fan of The Beatles. He acquired a snare drum and high hats by trading supermarket stamps his mom collected, allowing him to play along with Beatles records. At 13, his grandmother gave him a full drum set, which he expanded to match the size of Keith Moon's kit, who was his drumming hero. "Jeff got his mom to trade her stamps for a snare drum and a set of high hats so he could play along with his Beatles records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Mental Health Challenges
podcast.body: Joey Ramone suffered from mental health challenges beginning in his teenage years, for which he received psychiatric care. These early struggles contributed to his unique and often fragile public persona. "He suffered from some mental health challenges stemming from when he was a teenager. He did receive some psychiatric care when he was younger."

podcast.body: Joey Ramone experienced severe heartbreak when Linda, whom he believed was "the one," left him for his bandmate Johnny Ramone and subsequently married Johnny. This event led to a lasting estrangement, with Joey reportedly never forgiving either of them and ceasing to speak with Johnny for over a decade despite their continued band membership. podcast.title: Marfan Syndrome
podcast.body: He had Marfan Syndrome, a genetic connective tissue disorder that accounted for his tall, spindly physique and curved spine. "as well as a genetic condition of the body's connected tissue called Marfan Syndrome. This explains why he was so tall and spindly and had the curve spine."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marfan Syndrome Diagnosis
podcast.body: Joey also had Marfan Syndrome, a genetic disorder affecting connective tissue. This condition often results in individuals being very tall and thin with long limbs, fingers, and toes, and can lead to scoliosis and certain heart and circulatory issues. The syndrome's characteristic height made his fall more dangerous, contributing to the severity of his injuries. "People with Marfan's tend to be very tall and very thin with long limbs, fingers and toes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Marfan Syndrome and OCD
podcast.body: Joey Ramone had Marfan Syndrome, a genetic disorder, and was notably tall at six feet six inches. In addition to this, he suffered from a severe case of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), which made it incredibly difficult for him to leave his apartment due to compulsive checking behaviors, such as ensuring the stove was off or the door was locked. Even simple actions like stepping off a curb required multiple repetitions to satisfy the compulsion. "Joey Ramone was even taller at six six. He also had Marfan's."

podcast.title: OCD and Indirect Cause of Death
podcast.body: Joey Ramone's obsessive-compulsive disorder indirectly contributed to his death. Already battling lymphoma, a condition kept largely secret in the music world, he broke his hip after slipping on ice in December 2000. This incident occurred because he felt compelled to return to his doctor's office to re-check the door lock, following an appointment, and couldn't shake the nagging feeling once he got home. "And this OCD indirectly led to his death."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: OCD's Role in His Death
podcast.body: In December 2000, Joey was in remission from lymphoma. On an icy cold December 30th, 2000, he was overcome by an OCD compulsion to re-check a door across town. While leaving his apartment to fulfill this urge, he slipped on ice and broke his hip badly, an injury exacerbated by bones weakened and brittle from chemotherapy. This required hospitalization and removal from his anti-lymphoma medication, leading to the return of the lymphoma and overwhelming his immune system, ultimately causing his death on April 15, 2001. "But then one icy cold day after Christmas 2000, it was December 30th, 2000 to be exact. He was overcome by this feeling that he hadn't closed a door properly on the other side of town."

podcast.title: Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone suffered from obsessive compulsive disorder, which affected him throughout his life and reportedly exasperated his bandmates and managers. His OCD manifested in specific rituals, such as needing to step on and off a curb a certain number of times before proceeding, or touching objects in his apartment multiple times before leaving. These rituals often caused him to be late for band rehearsals and recording sessions. On one occasion, after landing in London, he wanted to immediately return home because he felt he had not exited his apartment door correctly. "It became reasonably well known that Joey suffered from obsessive compulsive disorder, which plagued him to the end and drove both his bandmates and his managers nuts. It was small things like having to step on and off a curb X number of times before he felt he could go on. He had a number of other rituals like touching various things in his apartment a certain number of times before he felt he could leave. This ended up making him late for things like rehearsals and recording sessions. There was also a time the band landed in London and Joey wanted to immediately turn around because he didn't walk out of his apartment door quite correctly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
podcast.body: Joey Ramone suffered from a severe case of OCD, which manifested in ritualistic behaviors like repeatedly checking his apartment door or stepping on and off a curb a specific number of times before moving on. Doctors, lacking modern understanding of the condition, once told him he would never be able to care for himself, and he was hospitalized at least once as a result. "It was something that was always there and he always had to struggle with. These voices in his head would say, you didn't close the door right, you got to do it again, and he would do it 20 times until it was right."

This surgical intervention prevented him from taking his chemotherapy drugs for lymphoma, leading to further complications that ultimately proved fatal. He died on April 15, 2001. podcast.title: Transition from Drummer to Singer – Founding The Ramones
podcast.body: In early 1974, Jeff Hyman was playing drums and singing in a band called Sniper. He then connected with John Cummings (guitar) and Douglas Colvin (bass), forming a new group that played its first gig on March 30, 1974. However, Hyman's drumming was too loud and fast for the band, and he proved to be a better singer than his bandmates. He moved to frontman, adopting the name Joey Ramone, while a friend named Tommy took over on a $100 drum set. "Jeff moved down front and became the singer and a friend named Tommy was forced to keep time using a hundred dollar drum set."

xref.title: Deaths of Original Members (2001-2014)
xref.body: The original lineup of the Ramones tragically passed away over a 13-year period: Joey Ramone in 2001, Dee Dee Ramone in 2002, Johnny Ramone in 2004, and Tommy Ramone in 2014, marking the end of an era for the seminal punk band. "He was the first of the original Ramones to die. Base player DD Ramon died of a heroin overdose the following summer. Whereas Johnny Ramon lost his fight with prostate cancer in September 2004, and drummer Tommy Ramon was taken by Bile Duck Cancer in the summer of 2014."

xref.title: Final Moments and Last Song (April 2001)
xref.body: On April 15, 2001, a month before his 50th birthday, Joey Ramone, nearing the end of his life at New York's Presbyterian Hospital, asked to listen to U2's song "In a Little While" from their album "All That You Can't Leave Behind" on a boombox beside his bed. Those present reported that he passed away just as the song concluded. "He asked to listen to a song in the boom box that was next to his bed at New York's Presbyterian Hospital. It was you two's in a little while, a song from the all that you can't leave behind album. Those who were with him at the time say that just as the song ended, Joey passed away."

xref.title: Death by Heroin Overdose (Summer 2002)
xref.body: Dee Dee Ramone, the bassist for the Ramones, tragically died of a heroin overdose in the summer following Joey Ramone's death. "Base player DD Ramon died of a heroin overdose the following summer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's OCD – Lifelong Battle Barely Acknowledged, Finally Confirmed on 2002 Solo Album
xref.body: Joey Ramone suffered from obsessive-compulsive disorder that preceded the formation of the Ramones and is cited by those close to him as a major reason he was so shy, awkward, and withdrawn in private. His OCD manifested in compulsive repetitive behaviors — stepping off and on a curb dozens of times, repeating words over and over driven by voices in his head — and he was hospitalized at least once when it became unmanageable. Despite this, Joey vehemently denied having OCD whenever it was raised publicly, and the subject was almost never discussed. As he came to terms with his cancer and mortality, he relented slightly, and in the song "Like a Drug I Never Did Before" on his 2002 posthumous solo album *Don't Worry About Me*, he addressed his lifelong battle with OCD — the only time he ever mentioned it in his music. "This is the only time he ever brought it up in his music."

xref.title: D.D. Ramone's Original Vocal Role
xref.body: D.D. Ramone became the main songwriter and lyricist for the Ramones for 15 years, despite his playing style consisting of long runs of the same notes. His spirit and raw energy were more impactful than technical prowess. "D.D. became the main songwriter and the lyricist for the Ramones for 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Enduring Animosity
xref.body: Despite Johnny Ramone and Linda Danielle marrying in 1984, The Ramones remained together and continued touring until 1996. Joey Ramone did not speak to Linda again until 1993, and he and Johnny almost never spoke again until the band's breakup. The feud was intense and quiet, prioritizing the band's business over personal issues. Johnny did not contact Joey when he was dying in early 2000 nor attend his funeral. "Joey didn't speak to Linda again until 1993. And Joey and Johnny almost never spoke again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fifteen-Year Feud Between Joey and Johnny
xref.body: Joey Ramone and Johnny Ramone, despite being in the same band and sharing all aspects of their professional lives, did not speak to each other for 15 years. This was largely due to Joey's girlfriend, Linda, leaving him for Johnny, whom she later married. Their political differences (Joey liberal, Johnny Republican) also contributed to the tension. "Joey's girlfriend Linda left him for Johnny whom she later married. The tension and the jealousy was unbelievable and it lasted more than 15 years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and Lineup Change – Drummer to Frontman
xref.body: The Ramones were formed in early 1974, with Jeff Hyman (later Joey Ramone) on drums, John Cummings (later Johnny Ramone) on guitar, and Douglas Colvin (later D.D. Ramone) on bass. Their first gig was on March 30, 1974. Due to Jeff's powerful, fast drumming style and his superior singing ability, he transitioned to lead vocalist, with a friend named Tommy taking over on drums using a basic $100 kit. "This arrangements worked out pretty good Especially after John became Johnny and Douglas became D.D. and Jeff adopted the name Joey and they all adopted the same last name Ramon."

xref.title: Inspiration and Band Formation
xref.body: Joseph Marciano Armstrong, nicknamed Joey after Joey Ramone, was born on February 28th, 1995. He decided to form his own band, Emily's Army, with a friend named Cole after they watched the movie "School of Rock" starring Jack Black. "And on February 28th, 1995, Joseph Marciano Armstrong came into the world. He's called Joey after Joey Ramon. Joey finally decided to form his own band after he and his buddy Cole saw School of Rock with Jack Black for the first time. That group was known as Emily's Army."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Internal Struggles and Resilience
xref.body: The Ramones endured various internal challenges, including members' drug habits, personality clashes, alcoholism, and Joey Ramone's obsessive-compulsive disorder, yet they remained committed to their music. "The bands survived through drug habits, personality clashes, alcoholism, and even joy Ramones obsessive compulsive disorder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Attraction to Women from Mental Hospitals (Unspecified Period)
xref.body: Joey Ramone, who suffered from OCD and underwent electro-shock treatment for his own psychiatric issues, was rumored to have had a preference for dating women from mental hospitals. It was alleged that he would get drunk and frequent these institutions, stating that "the girls were all loose there," and supposedly fell in love with a woman who received weekly electro-shock therapy. This attraction is linked to his own experiences with mental health, which also influenced lyrics he wrote for the Ramones, such as "Gimme Gimme Shock Treatment." "Apparently Joey had a thing for a while for girls from mental hospitals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Capitalism
xref.body: Despite embodying the image of an "archetypical punk," Joey Ramone was, in fact, a hardcore capitalist. In the years leading up to his death, he became very skilled at stock trading over the internet. He reportedly amassed a considerable fortune by diligently following the Wall Street Journal, watching CNBC, and utilizing his online trading account.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Death and Memorial
xref.body: Diagnosed with lymphoma in 1995, Joey Ramone's cancer worsened after he broke his hip in a fall in late 2000, which necessitated coming off his chemotherapy. He died on April 15, 2001, just one month before his 50th birthday. The corner of East Second Street and Bowery, near CBGB and his last apartment, is now officially named "Joey Ramone Place." He is buried in Hillside Cemetery in New Jersey, overlooking Manhattan. "he died on April 15, 2001, a month short of his 50th birthday. The corner of East Second Street in Bahri is now officially known as Joey Ramon Place."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Early Glam Phase
xref.body: Around his 21st birthday, Joey became deeply immersed in glam culture, idolizing David Bowie and Alice Cooper. He would dress in satin jumpsuits adorned with rhinestones and wear knee-high platform boots, which exaggerated his height to six feet eight inches. "He also became a big fan of Alice Cooper. His first real band was called Sniper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's First Band
xref.body: This was Joey Ramone's first "real band," where he performed as the singer under the name Jeff Starship. They were active from 1972 to 1974 and specialized in writing songs about "weirdness and perversion." No known recordings exist of Joey Ramone's version of the band. "His first real band was called Sniper. Joey was their singer, going by the name Jeff Starship. And he specialized in running songs about weirdness and perversion."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Health Issues
xref.body: Unknown to most at the time of their retirement, Joey Ramone was suffering from lymphoma. This illness, combined with ongoing internal band tensions and his historical predisposition to colds and flu, made dealing with the rigors of performing increasingly difficult and contributed to the decision to end the band. "What we didn't know at the time was that Joy Ramon was sick. He'd been working through lymphoma and was finding it increasingly hard to deal with the rigors of performing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Marfan Syndrome
xref.body: Jeffrey Hyman (Joey Ramone) suffered from Marfan Syndrome, an inherited disorder affecting connective tissue, leading to his tall, gangly physique with long limbs and fingers. This condition can also cause serious heart problems and, if untreated, typically limits life expectancy to 32 years. "Young Jeffrey grew up with all sorts of health problems. He was tall and gauky as the result of something called Marfan Syndrome, which is an inherited disorder living on chromosome 15 that messes with connective tissue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's OCD
xref.body: Diagnosed with OCD at age 18, Joey Ramone's life was plagued by the disorder. This manifested in specific rituals, such as needing to step on and off a curb a certain number of times before moving on, and elaborate routines required before leaving his apartment. "For example, he sometimes had to step on and off a curb a prescribed number of times before he could move on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey Ramone's Preference for Dating Women from Mental Institutions
xref.body: Joey Ramone had a documented pattern of seeking out women from psychiatric institutions. By his own admission, he found these women interesting, and he reportedly spent time hanging around outside mental health facilities while drinking, describing the patients as "all loose." One relationship was with a woman who received weekly electroshock therapy. None of this was ever discussed publicly during his lifetime. "Joey's thing was girls from mental hospitals."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Decades-Long Feud (Post-Linda Breakup)
xref.body: Joey Ramone was deeply heartbroken when his girlfriend Linda left him for his bandmate Johnny Ramone, whom she later married. Joey never forgave either of them, and despite remaining in the same band until the end, Joey and Johnny reportedly never spoke to each other after Linda changed relationships, leading to a decade of silence between them during band activities. "The story is that although they were in the same band together to the end, Joey and Johnny never spoke a word to each other after Linda changed teams."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey and Johnny Ramone's Long-Standing Feud
xref.body: For much of the Ramones' existence until their official end in August 1996, Joey Ramone and Johnny Ramone did not speak to each other due to Joey's girlfriend, Linda, breaking up with him and subsequently marrying Johnny. "And for much of that time, they never spoke, because Joey's girlfriend Linda broke up with him and started dating Johnny."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joey's Name Change
xref.body: Jeffrey Hyman decided to change his stage name to Joey Ramone, believing it sounded "much cooler" than Jeff Ramon, further cementing the band's unified identity. "The last change came when Jeffrey decided that he'd rather go by Joey. Joey Ramon just sounded so much cooler than Jeff Ramon."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Conservative Politics
xref.body: Johnny Ramone was known as a hardcore Republican, one of the most conservative punk rockers. He openly admired and worshipped Ronald Reagan. This political stance often put him at odds with Joey Ramone, especially when he had to perform anti-Reagan songs written by Joey, such as "Bonzo Goes to Bitburg."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Johnny Ramone's Post-Mortem Sentiments
xref.body: Johnny Ramone expressed his lack of desire to interact with Joey Ramone even in death, stating he wouldn't want Joey at his funeral and wouldn't want to hear from him if he were dying, preferring to be left alone by friends. "I was in California, said Johnny. I wasn't going to travel all the way to New York, but I wouldn't have gone anyway. I wouldn't want him coming to my funeral and I wouldn't want to hear from him if I were dying."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Love Triangle and Intra-Band Feud
xref.body: In 1976, Joey Ramone met 16-year-old fan Linda Danielle from Queens at CBGB. They reconnected in Los Angeles a couple of years later and became a couple, with Linda joining The Ramones on tour. Johnny Ramone, who initially made Linda sit in the back of the van, eventually discovered common ground with her (neither drank or did drugs, she liked to cook, he liked home-cooked meals) and they became best friends. Joey and Linda became engaged, but after a dispute over a ring price, Johnny realized he was in love with Linda. Johnny intimidated Joey, who hated conflict, leading Linda to move towards Johnny over the next 18 months. They broke up, and Johnny and Linda became a couple in the early 1980s, marrying in 1984. "In 1976, just as the Ramones were starting to become known, Joey met a young 16-year-old fan named Linda Danielle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Musical Offspring
xref.body: Billy Joe Armstrong has two sons, Joseph Marciano Armstrong (Joey), born February 28th, 1995, and named after Joey Ramone, and Jacob Danger Armstrong, born September 12th, 1998. Both sons have followed their father into music. "And on February 28th, 1995, Joseph Marciano Armstrong came into the world. He's called Joey after Joey Ramon. Another song, Jacob Danger Armstrong. Yeah, his middle name is Danger. Came along on September 12th of 1998. Both boys took after their father."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Original Lineup and Roles
xref.body: The initial lineup included Jeff Hyman (Joey Ramone) on drums, a "6'6-inch skinny guy" and "OCD-suffering refugee from a failed band called Sniper." Their first gig was in March. By July, Jeff Hyman moved to lead vocals because he was a better singer than drummer, and their manager, Tommy (Tommy Ramone), a recording engineer who had worked with Jimi Hendrix, took over on drums. "Their drummer was a 6'6-inch skinny guy named Jeff Heimann, an OCD-suffering refugee from a failed band called Sniper."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Political and Personal Ideology Clash
xref.body: Joey Ramone was described as a liberal with sympathies for hippie types and progressive outlooks, while Johnny Ramone was conservative, supporting Ronald Reagan and disliking hippies. Despite these opposing views, they managed to form the band and find common ground in music. "Joey Ramon was a liberal sort of dude with sympathies for hippie types and those with progressive outlooks on life. The stars, Joey Ramon hated hippies. He was about as conservative as it got when it came to politics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-Ramones Band – Jeff Hyman's Role
xref.body: Jeff Hyman, who would later become Joey Ramone, formed a band called Sniper. In this group, he not only played the drums but also served as the singer, showcasing his dual talents before the formation of The Ramones. "Finally, he formed a band called Sniper and as well as playing the drums he ended up being the singer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Reunion Performances
xref.body: Following their rediscovery, the band was enticed to reunite and even performed at one of Joey Ramone's Memorial birthday parties, a testament to their newly recognized status in punk history. "The band was enticed to reunite and even performed at one of Joey Ramones Memorial birthday parties."

xref.title: Shared Bills with Ramones
xref.body: In 1975, Tuftarts performed on bills with the Ramones at CBGB. The band was also described as being "sort of a direct descendant of sniper," Joey Ramone's old band, indicating a lineage within the punk scene. "Other times, they'd be on a bill with a talking heads or blondey or a band called Tuftarts, which, if you want to get technical about it, was sort of a direct descendant of sniper, Joey's old band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sire Records Signing - Trailblazers
xref.body: Joey Ramone stated that Sire Records "understood us best" and that the band wouldn't get "lost in the shuffle" by signing with them, despite later interest from bigger labels. The Ramones considered themselves "sort of the trailblazers," conducting the first national tour and inspiring other bands to get signed after witnessing their success. "We decided to go with Sire because we felt the seamless style understood us best and that we wouldn't get lost in the shuffle being on a major company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Stage Names and Image
xref.body: To symbolize their unity and brotherhood, all band members adopted the surname "Ramone." Jeff Hyman became Joey Ramone, Douglas Colvin became Dee Dee Ramone, John Cummings became Johnny Ramone, and Tommy kept his first name. They also adopted a uniform "tough leather jacket and jeans look." "Everybody adopted a tough leather jacket and jeans look, and everybody had a stage name. Jeff became Joey. Douglas was DD, John was Johnny, and Tommy stayed Tommy. And as a symbol of their brotherhood, they all adopted the same last name, Ramone."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: The Teapot Incident
xref.body: Backstage at the Capitol Theater in Passaic, New Jersey, Joey Ramone, suffering from a cold, rigged a makeshift humidifier using a teapot on a hot plate in the dressing room. The teapot "ended up blowing up in Joey's face," causing second and third-degree burns. Despite his injuries, he was rushed to the hospital for treatment and then returned to the venue to perform the show. "Somehow it ended up blowing up in Joey's face and engsculting water all over him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
